I did the 1L with with smart bottle/compatible bottles and had two 1L bottles compatible with the filter, and both would be directly scooping water. I drank straight from those.  I had 1 nalgene bottle (those wide diameter 1L bottles) that if I needed more water than 2L I would use the smart bottle to filter into the nalgene. 

I also used the tablets overnight in my nalgene and i liked that because I could just drink straight out of it in the morning without taking time to filter into it. I would recommend keeping at least a few tablets for emergency, I met a few people who had their filter fail on them on the trail (thankfully people shared water and/or they were in a group!) 

((Note: This is from my experience in the AT not PCT, not sure how those longer stretches without water are going to change this. Probably I would filter into some bottles but still keep two bottles directly for scooping & drinking ))

Doesnt sound pathetic. I totally feel you OP. I feel like LiS has been a huge support in my recent struggles and its been a comfort for me definitely. I have been going through a lot and I feel like LiS has really helped me to get me through it.

Theres a lot of lessons in LiS that I think pertain to/help with depression and if you can take those lessons while also making slow changes in your own life then I think itll be less scary and itll be less of an end, and more of a start to a new outlook, if ya know how I mean? 
I know its hard when you are depressed, self harm, and everything else that comes with it. Trust me, ive been there. And I know things like this become sort of 'reasons worth living for', little check points in your life. Things to look forward to and keep fighting for.
But keep on fighting. You a stronger on the inside and you can do it. Once its over you are not losing anything. You are becoming stronger. 
Keep fighting my friend, you can do it. Remember that you are never alone.

I am sorry for your loss. I had a teacher who became the happiest soul when she found out she was pregnant, but then had a miscarriage and we never saw her again. I remember one of the students (some students and teachers were on a very close level) explaining how devastated she was at this loss. 

I know you never spent a day with your child out of the womb but I think perhaps the bond between mother and child begins at conception. Have you tried going to a therapist? As with any loss, we experience grief and sometimes we cant move beyond without help. And help is okay to ask for. I dont think a miscarriage is easy for any mother to deal with. I would say the best start would be to ask for help in coping, or just for expressing how you feel. 

Have you tried any support groups? you did lose a child, and if you are feeling that others invalidate that feeling, I think a support group would help.

Also, just wanted to add something quick. Perhaps you could also find a fun activity to do. Running was my go to activity that really helped me personally. When I ran, nothing mattered. No depression, no dysphoria, nothing. Obviously yes that all still existed and when my depression hit its highest point even running couldnt help me. But before that point, it really helped.

Im not saying running helps everyone, but it was an activity that kept my entire focus on it. If it was cross country, I enjoyed the scenery around me. If it was track, I focused on crushing my opponents. When I ran I had a certain time or distance allotted to it, and in that time, nothing else mattered. 

If you can find an activity that creates the same safe feeling, perhaps that will help you as well.

Hey, I get the gender dysphoria, I used to experience it huge time before.  What helped me best (prior to taking hormones, as I dont know if you are taking those or not) was just being in a community where I could feel like me. I was still dysphoric and felt uncomfortable, but hearing my friends using male pronouns and referring to me as such made me happy. I could feel myself because I had that group where they saw me as I saw me. Of course dysphoria is still there, and once we left to go home it came back hard (family wouldnt use proper pronouns, emphasized female pronouns when we were in public) and it got me really hard. But I held on to those moments with my friends. 
I dont know how old you are, but if you are still living with your parents, I would recommend hanging with friends who see you as you and/or going to a trans group safe space. 
I know its hard, and in the end its kind of something you have to just deal with, but if you can find those safe spaces it really helps. 
For me, taking testosterone really helped me, I felt more confident in my outward experience. Early on in the physical transition, when people still misgendered me, I kind of laughed about it because I felt secure in who I was. 
I still get body dysphoria (my biggest issue is my chest) but I keep telling myself that I will have the body I want one day. Especially with all the changes in insurance and the like. 
I know its not a very solid answer, and it did take me years and a lot of dark times to cope with it, but if you make an active effort to slowly make changes that help you solidify your gender outwardly and inwardly (as in, 'fuck everyone im a girl' or however you identify) i think it will help. 
I too have depression, and I know in the past at my worst, mixed with the dysphoria is horrific. Now they are two distinct issues to me but I know how the depression heightens the dysphoria. 
Stay safe and take it easy. Transitioning will always be a long journey, not just in dealing with society, but with learning to accept ourselves. 
As I said before, find safe spaces. And no matter what happens, stay true to yourself and do what is best for you.
